title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 19 (Subsidiary company not to hold shares in its holding company)

content.overview: Section 19 generally prohibits a subsidiary from holding shares in its holding company and prohibits the holding company from allotting or transferring its shares to the subsidiary. Any such allotment or transfer is void, subject to specified statutory exceptions.
content.glance: The core rule is a prohibition on cross-holding by a subsidiary in its holding company, subject to three specified exceptions and a limited voting consequence.
content.study: Section 19 addresses reciprocal shareholding between a holding company and its subsidiary. The basic rule is that a company cannot, directly or through nominees, hold shares in its holding company; correspondingly, the holding company cannot allot or transfer its shares to a subsidiary, and a prohibited allotment or transfer is void. The section preserves three situations: shares held by the subsidiary as legal representative of a deceased member; shares held as trustee; and shares already held before the subsidiary relationship arose. Voting is specially restricted for the third-category subsidiary holding: the subsidiary may vote only in respect of shares held as legal representative or trustee. For a holding company limited by guarantee or an unlimited company without share capital, references to shares are read as references to members' interests.

sections.heading: General prohibition
sections.body: A subsidiary cannot hold shares in its holding company, directly or through nominees; the holding company likewise cannot allot or transfer its shares to the subsidiary. A prohibited allotment or transfer is void.

sections.heading: Statutory exceptions
sections.body: The prohibition does not apply where the subsidiary holds the shares as legal representative of a deceased member, as trustee, or where the subsidiary was already a shareholder before it became a subsidiary.

sections.heading: Voting limitation
sections.body: The subsidiary has voting rights in the holding company only for shares held in the legal-representative or trustee capacities identified in the first two exceptions.

sections.heading: No-share-capital holding company
sections.body: Where the holding company is limited by guarantee or unlimited and has no share capital, references to shares are construed as references to members' interests.

sections.heading: Application test
sections.body: Establish the holding/subsidiary relationship, identify the manner and timing of the holding, test each exception, determine whether the allotment/transfer is void and apply the voting rule.

examples.title: Prohibited acquisition
examples.body: A subsidiary acquires shares in its holding company through a nominee after becoming a subsidiary. The transaction falls within the prohibition and the allotment/transfer is void.

examples.title: Pre-existing holding
examples.body: A company already held shares in another company before becoming its subsidiary. This is within the express exception, subject to the section's voting limitation.

examples.title: Trust holding
examples.body: A subsidiary holds shares as trustee. The trust capacity is expressly recognised as an exception.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 19 addresses reciprocal shareholding between a holding company and its subsidiary. The basic rule is that a company cannot, directly or through nominees, hold shares in its holding company; correspondingly, the holding company cannot allot or transfer its shares to a subsidiary, and a prohibited allotment or transfer is void. The section preserves three situations: shares held by the subsidiary as legal representative of a deceased member; shares held as trustee; and shares already held before the subsidiary relationship arose. Voting is specially restricted for the third-category subsidiary holding: the subsidiary may vote only in respect of shares held as legal representative or trustee. For a holding company limited by guarantee or an unlimited company without share capital, references to shares are read as references to members' interests.

Key statutory components:
1. General prohibition — A subsidiary cannot hold shares in its holding company, directly or through nominees; the holding company likewise cannot allot or transfer its shares to the subsidiary. A prohibited allotment or transfer is void.
2. Statutory exceptions — The prohibition does not apply where the subsidiary holds the shares as legal representative of a deceased member, as trustee, or where the subsidiary was already a shareholder before it became a subsidiary.
3. Voting limitation — The subsidiary has voting rights in the holding company only for shares held in the legal-representative or trustee capacities identified in the first two exceptions.
4. No-share-capital holding company — Where the holding company is limited by guarantee or unlimited and has no share capital, references to shares are construed as references to members' interests.
5. Application test — Establish the holding/subsidiary relationship, identify the manner and timing of the holding, test each exception, determine whether the allotment/transfer is void and apply the voting rule.
